newsitem.title: USA: Integon likely to attract buyers.
newsitem.headline: Integon likely to attract buyers.

text.p: Auto insurer Integon Corp is likely to attract interest from a number of U.S. property-casualty companies despite its poor earnings performance the last few quarters.
Although the earnings have been a disappointment, the problems should be fairly easy to correct and rather short-lived in nature, one Wall Street analyst said.
"Once you've identified the problem, the corrective actions are not all that difficult to recognize," he said.

Insurers that may have an interest in North Carolina-based Integon, which specializes in non-standard, or high-risk, automobile insurance, could include Travelers Property Casualty Corp, The Hartford, CNA Financial Corp, American International Group Inc, Allstate Corp and Progressive Corp, analysts said.
CNA was not immediately available for comment.
Travelers Property Casualty, AIG, The Hartford, Allstate, and Progressive declined comment.
But Progressive and Allstate, which already have thriving non-standard auto businesses of their own, may not have much incentive to buy troubled Integon, Conning and Co analyst Gary Ransom said.
"I would say it's not going to be another non-standard company," Ransom said.
But any of the other big multiline insurers are possible buyers, he said.
"I think there are a lot of interested parties for almost anything that comes to the marketplace," another analyst said.
"I would be shocked if Integon was left at the altar now that they've put themselves up there," he added.
Integon's move comes after the company reported a surprising first quarter loss of $2.21 a share.
Excluding additions to reserves and writeoffs, the company had a first quarter loss of $0.33 a share. That compares to analysts' First Call consensus estimate of a loss of $0.03 a share.
Integon said it experienced greater than anticipated physical damage loss activity related the 1996 accident year.
In addition, the company decided it needed to further strengthen loss reserves following an in-depth review.
The company also turned in surprisingly poor results in the 1996 fourth quarter and began to show signs of trouble in the 1996 third quarter, Ransom said.

Although the company has been losing money and had to add $27.3 million after tax to its loss reserves, analysts said they did not believe Integon was looking for a buyer because it was in immediate financial trouble.
"I don't think they're backed into a corner at this point," Ransom said. "Although it is pretty bad."
He said the company told analysts in its conference call that it had sufficient cash available through bank lines to meet its current capital needs.
"I don't think they're in financial distress," the other analyst said.

But, the company is without a chief executive officer and its competitive position in the non-standard auto market has been compromised and therefore it "just might be better off under the wings of someone else," he said.
